newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ILO targets intolerable forms of child labour.
newsitem.headline: ILO targets intolerable forms of child labour.

text.p: The most harmful forms of child labour -- slavery, debt bondage, prostitution and work in hazardous industries -- will be the target of a two-day international conference in Amsterdam on Wednesday.

The International Labour Organisation (ILO), which is co-hosting the conference with the Dutch government, estimates that nearly a third of the world's 250 million child labourers work under dangerous or harmful conditions.
Their plight will be discussed in Amsterdam by some 200 government ministers, labour union leaders, officials of employer organisations and representatives of working children.
"These intolerable forms of child labour are the first concern for all of us," Dutch Social Affairs Minister Ad Melkert told reporters at a pre-conference briefing on Tuesday.
"Referring to other cultures, customs and traditions can never be an excuse."
The U.N. Children's Fund (Unicef) says most, but not all, working children live in developing countries.
In India, Labour Ministry officials say 18 million children are at work rather than at school, while children's-rights activists put the figure at around 55 million.

An ILO report prepared for the conference says tens of millions of child labourers in South Asia are kept in slavery or under forced labour systems such as debt bondage, where children work to pay off a family obligation.
The report notes the increasing sexual exploitation of children and its terrible effects.
"Case studies reveal a trauma so deep that many such children are unable to return to a normal life. Many others die before adulthood," the ILO says.
The problem is not confined to Asia.
Unicef estimates that in Africa one child in three works and in Latin America the figure is one in five.
The conference is seen as a step towards the drafting of a new international convention on the worst forms of child exploitation, ILO Director-General Michel Hansenne said.

"We want a new convention in a global context that will be possible for all the ILO's members to ratify and to comply with, shall we say, the minimum rules of the game," he said. "The conference gives us a good opportunity to discuss this."
Developing countries will be well represented in Amsterdam, with the Labour ministers of India, Bangladesh, Brazil, Thailand, Tanzania and Egypt all due to attend.
A new agreement would complement rather than replace the ILO's current 1973 Minimum Age Convention, Deputy Director-General Karl Tapioli said.

"We are aiming to create a human rights instrument to set down certain basic principles. One would be that there are certain forms of child labour that are so intolerable they should be abolished immediately," he said.
Concerted action on child labour has long been complicated by a political dimension to the debate.
Developing nations are suspicious of Western interference in workers rights, fearing this will undermine their main comparative advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.
Some contend that Western nations are using the issue to disguise nascent protectionism and gain unfair trade advantages.
But while most oppose trade curbs linked to the issue, several affected countries have recently been stirred into action by growing international outrage.
In December, India said it had taken 150,000 child labourers out of hazardous industries under a plan to eliminate children from such jobs by 2002.
Bangladesh's garment industry, faced with U.S. import restrictions, now also says it is free of child labour.
Representatives of working children themselves will also be present at the conference.

Basrur Lakshmi, a domestic servant from the age of eight and now, at 17, an organiser for an Indian working childrens' union, told a meeting on Monday night that their participation was an important step.
"This is the very first time we have been invited to take part in decision making affecting our own lives," she said.
